opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's really the core motivation for a lot of this work. Right now, when we evaluate a model, we're mostly looking at inputs and outputs. You give it a prompt, you see what comes out, and you try to infer from a large number of those examples whether the model is doing what you want. That gets you pretty far, but it leaves a big blind spot: you can see *that* a model got something right or wrong, but not *why*.

The analogy I like is medicine. For a long time you could only observe symptoms, and you'd guess at causes. Once you have tools that let you look inside, like imaging and blood work, you can say "this is what's actually going on," and you can intervene much more precisely. Interpretability is trying to build that kind of tooling for models.

Concretely, if you can trace the intermediate steps a model takes on a given prompt, you start to see things like: is it actually doing multi-step reasoning, or pattern-matching to something that happens to correlate with the right answer? When it explains its reasoning in a chain of thought, does that explanation match the computation it actually ran, or is it a plausible story constructed after the fact? Those are very hard to answer from outputs alone, and they matter a lot for trust.

On the debugging side, take hallucinations. Instead of just noting that the model made up a fact, you can look at what happened internally. Maybe there's a mechanism that's supposed to say "I don't know this entity, I should decline," and something about the prompt suppressed it because the name looked familiar enough. Once you see that, you have a much more specific hypothesis about the failure mode, and you can check whether the same mechanism explains a whole class of errors rather than patching them one at a time.

The "macro-level" part is important too. Looking at individual neurons or single features is useful, but the real payoff comes when you can see how these pieces compose into circuits that implement a behavior, and then notice that the same circuit shows up across many prompts. That lets you move from anecdotes to something closer to a general understanding of how the model handles, say, arithmetic, or planning ahead when writing, or refusals.

I'd be honest that we're still early. The tools capture part of the computation, not all of it, and there's real work in validating that what we think we're seeing is what's actually happening, usually by intervening on those internal features and checking that the behavior changes the way we'd predict. But even partial visibility changes how you approach evaluation. It lets you ask better questions, and it gives you a way to catch problems that a benchmark would never reveal.

r001.rationale: The response proposes tracing internal computation and identifying circuits that implement high-level behaviors such as arithmetic, planning, or refusals.

r002.rationale: It proposes inspecting a mechanism involved in hallucinations, but does not describe checking whether the model formed internal connections between concepts expected to be related.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that right now, when a model does something weird, you're basically stuck doing black-box debugging. You see an input, you see an output, and you have to guess at what happened in between. And the way people do it today is they'll poke at the prompt, they'll try a bunch of variations, maybe they'll look at the attention patterns if they're feeling ambitious. But it's a very indirect process.

What a macro-level understanding gets you is something closer to what a software engineer has when they open up a debugger. You can actually trace the path from the input to the output and ask, okay, at which point did this go off the rails? So, for example, if a model is hallucinating a citation, is that because it genuinely represents some fact internally and then retrieves the wrong thing? Or is it because there's a circuit that's basically saying "I'm in a context where a citation is expected, so produce something citation-shaped," and the content was never grounded at all? Those are two very different failure modes, and they call for very different fixes. From the outside they look identical.

The other piece is on the evaluation side. Evals today are almost entirely behavioral. You test on a benchmark, you get a number, and you hope the benchmark is representative of what you care about. But the thing you actually care about is often the mechanism. Like, did the model learn to reason about this problem, or did it learn a shortcut that happens to work on your test distribution? If you can look inside and see that the model is using, say, a feature that tracks surface-level cues rather than the underlying structure, you've learned something your benchmark couldn't tell you. You've learned how it's going to fail before it fails.

And I'd say the "macro" part is important. A lot of interpretability work has been very micro, right? Individual neurons, individual attention heads. That's valuable, but it doesn't scale to the question of "why did the model do this thing on this prompt." What you want is a coarser description, something like, here are the handful of concepts the model was tracking, here's how they interacted, and here's the step where the decision got made. That's the level at which a human can actually form a hypothesis, test it, and intervene. So I think of it less as a replacement for behavioral evals and more as the thing that tells you where to look when the behavioral eval tells you something is wrong.

r001.rationale: The response proposes looking inside the model for features that track surface cues versus underlying structure, and describes identifying the concepts tracked, how they interact, and where a decision is made to evaluate behavior.

r002.rationale: It contrasts possible internal causes of a hallucinated citation and mentions concept interactions, but does not propose checking whether the model formed internal connections between concepts expected to be related.

astra-6.text:
I think it gives you another way to ask whether the model is doing what you intended. Usually, you evaluate a model by looking at its outputs: you give it a set of examples, measure how often it gets them right, and inspect the failures. That’s essential, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you why it’s getting something right, or when that behavior might break.

If you had a higher-level understanding of the mechanisms involved, you could start distinguishing between a model that uses the information you want it to use and one that relies on a shortcut. Imagine a classifier that performs well on your test set, but internally it’s mostly responding to something in the background rather than the object you care about. That gives you a concrete hypothesis about where it will fail, and you can design an evaluation to test that hypothesis.

The exciting part for debugging is moving from ‘Here are a hundred examples where something went wrong’ to ‘Maybe these failures share a mechanism.’ If you can identify that mechanism and intervene on it, you can test whether your explanation actually predicts the behavior. I wouldn’t see that as replacing behavioral evaluations. It would help us make those evaluations more targeted and understand what their results really tell us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding mechanisms and detecting shortcuts, but does not propose identifying internal components associated with high-level computational functions.

r002.rationale: It suggests looking for a shared mechanism behind failures, but does not propose checking whether the model formed internal connections between concepts expected to be related.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it gives you a way to move from observing a failure to forming a hypothesis about why it happened. You can evaluate a model on a benchmark and see that it gets certain examples wrong, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what to change.

If you have a higher-level understanding of the mechanisms involved—what information the model is using, how it’s combining that information, and what drives the final answer—you can start asking more targeted questions. Is it failing to retrieve something it knows? Is it relying on a shortcut? Is it applying a useful behavior in the wrong context?

And then, ideally, you can test those hypotheses. If you think a particular mechanism is responsible, can you intervene on it and predict how the behavior will change? That’s where this becomes useful for debugging. It also helps you design evaluations that probe the underlying failure mode, rather than just collecting more examples that happen to look like the original failure.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding mechanisms and testing a suspected mechanism, but does not propose identifying internal components tied to high-level computational functions.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the model retrieves information or relies on a shortcut, but does not propose checking for internal connections between concepts expected to be related.
